title: Most "vibecoders" aren't amateurs. A lot of them are laid-off industry pros
author: Usual_Importance8274
selftext:
There's no such thing as a true amateur vibecoder out there.

I keep seeing posts saying vibecoders are bad because most of them are amateurs with no game dev experience, no programming knowledge, no art or modeling skills, and so on.

I think that's completely wrong (at least from where I'm standing). Here's why, and it's pretty easy to picture: companies are using AI to maximize productivity and lay people off.

And it's not just juniors getting cut. Experienced professionals are being let go too. They can't find new jobs, so they turn around and use the same AI to build their own projects.

It's a vicious cycle.

None of these people are really amateurs. A lot of the so-called "AI slop" projects aren't actually slop. They're complete, with every element a real game needs. The only reason we can tell AI was involved is that they ship on the web, running on WGPU.

So I feel like most of these posts are criticizing the wrong people. Vibecoders aren't newcomers. Many of them are industry veterans. The only reason they can't hide their AI usage is that their old workflows were tied to Unreal or Unity, and LLMs just aren't that strong with those engines. The models tend to push projects toward open-source, web-based stacks, because that's what they've been trained on the most. Unreal is the big exception here: it's so UI-driven that understanding the codebase alone doesn't let an agent actually get much done.

comments.author: Brapchu
comments.body:
>Vibecoders aren't newcomers. Many of them are industry veterans.

Even as an "industry veteran" you can be shit and it doesn't mean you should be absolved of delivering vibecoded slop.

>None of these people are really amateurs. A lot of the so-called "AI slop" projects aren't actually slop. They're complete, with every element a real game needs. The only reason we can tell AI was involved is that they ship on the web, running on WGPU.

replies.author: Turbulent_Peace_8398
replies.body: Yeah I’ve been making AAA-games since like 2007 before I got laid off early this year and I can for sure say I’m vibecoding ALOT of small supersloppy projects simply to output and re-learn as much as possible fast, and also to have a bit of fun and not take everything so seriously for once. if a project sticks and I feel it’s worth to treat it as something more than a quick prototype, it’ll most probably become non-slop

comments.body: Most are vibe coders. People not caring and just making software. Few are craftsmen and that is what matters. Are you a game dev, or looking to make money. You cant seriously be both. Only game devs will survive this, even strong cs engineers will fail compared to true dreamers.

Using AI assisted coding is different from vibecoding. 

Most of the experienced devs will care about their outputs. Also it's fine to vibecode small things (eg a local tool for testing)

A tier 1, professional solution, can be done with Claude and codex but it does not mean it was vibecoded

comments.author: SanjaESC
comments.body: How do people come up with such brain dead takes and also who cares?

comments.author: MakingSoulStudio
comments.body:
I'm a real vibe coder who started without knowing how to code at all.



Thanks to that, I've been cranking out AI slop, failing, and growing from it.



I've found that vibe coding isn't everything. If the planning wobbles, the game's direction gets blurry. If you don't understand the development process, you drift off course and get lost along the way. And because I knew nothing about game dev, I've even done ridiculous things like starting to polish the moment development began.



That's how I'm learning and growing.

comments.author: Enderoth
comments.body:
I’m 100% not an industry pro. Or in the industry at all.

I just started making the game I wanted to play. Been prompting my way to victory for a few weeks. Honestly, its been fun to work on. I did not, however, expect I’d need to edit so many spreadsheets or test for so many bugs. Then again, that’s type 2 fun.

My game has a pretty satisfying loop. Now I’m adding content and bug squashing. No code experience at all.

comments.author: ConsistentAnalysis35
comments.body:
"Industry pros and veterans" yeah sure. I've worked with a couple of those pro game devs who were in the business of making cheap mobile slop in Unity. Didn't even really knew C#, much less the architecture of a game engine.

Yeah, professionals much. I would bet there's a good chunk of amateur modders who can run circles around half of the professional gamedev industry.

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
I would go as far and say that we have a lot of children and teenagers here too. I remember myself at that age getting into game modding.

Such a luxury to have AI to ask questions to. I had to go to the library to find stuff. YouTube barely existed and there were no tutorials on there. Just videos of people's weddings and some comedy and sports.

replies.author: hateborne
replies.body: Just think, a little bit later and you could have had the luxury of stack overflow's gauntlet of insults, "closed as duplicate" while linked to a completely unrelated thread, and the most toxic people on the planet outside playing a competitive online game. /s

replies.author: EliasWick
replies.body:
Haha well, now 20 years later, I do understand them and why they did what they did. It was toxic, but people never read the rules of conduct and so on. For the most part I got great responses for all my questions. The issue is terminology and if you didn't know what you were looking for it took forever to find and you might get a closed or duplicate post due to you not understanding the synonyms.

For the time I get it, but I did like the order a little bit. I don't like what they've done on Reddit where you can be completely anonymous and post without people being able to see your older posts. I think people should stand for what they write and their experiences.

Sorry for going off track. Yes, that was a tough period, I might have posted at least 20 duplicate posts, but what is a 14 year old to do when he's making his .net, and don't understand OOP.

comments.author: Keltanes
comments.body:
I'm an amateur coder. I've written a few small apps to control devices for automation, etc.

Now I'm vibe-coding a physical collectible card game into an app (already working pretty well). I'm also already in pre-production for a real 3D game based on an original concept with my own ideas for world-building and gameplay, etc. My main challenge (endboss) will be the 3D assets and animation.

There's no chance in hell I could have pulled that off with zero programming experience (and I also wouldn't have been able to pull that off without AI).

Despite all that and the patent I authored, and the numerous exploits and patches I've dropped recently and over the decades.  The only people who call my apps slop are those who can't, can't code, can't architect, can't fathom that one person can do this thing that quickly.   TDLR to me it reeks of performance anxiety.

comments.author: mars_santa
comments.body:
I am a low-skill hobby coder with several years of experience working with human development teams. I see the difference between working directly with AI and working with seasoned professional developers, but I don't have a team for my projects so it works for me until I do.

I also watched seasoned developers become seasoned developers who also use AI and it is way different from how I use it for my projects. They benefit from it, I rely on it. That is a huge difference and their final products are going to be superior.
